hero.highlight.text: it doesn't have to go to the model every time.

hero.takeaway.text: Put the full text of every skill in the system prompt and every request has to carry all of it. Put in only a catalog and let the model fetch a skill's text with load_skill when it needs it, and the resident context is much smaller, at the price of an extra tool round trip. Whether the model picks the right skill depends on the one-line description in the catalog.

concepts.01-skill.title.text: A procedure written for the model

concepts.01-skill.description.text: A skill is a written procedure for the model. In this lesson each skill is a file in SKILL.md format: between the two --- lines at the top are a name and a description, and the body below gives the steps, the output format, and a self-check list.

concepts.02-full.description.text: Put the description and body of every skill into the system prompt. One request is enough to finish the task, but every request carries all the bodies, whether the task needs them or not.

concepts.03-disclose.description.text: Progressive disclosure: the system prompt holds only a skill catalog, one line of name and description per skill. When the model needs a skill it calls load_skill, and the body enters the next request as a tool result.

concepts.04-description.title.text: The description decides whether a skill gets picked

concepts.04-description.description.text: With on-demand loading, the model can only go by the description in the catalog to decide which skill to load. Not loading when it should is a missed trigger; loading when it shouldn't is a false trigger.

section-1.title.text: The more procedures, the longer the system prompt

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: If you write every procedure into the system prompt, every request carries all of them, whether this request needs them or not. The system prompts in the earlier lessons were only a sentence or two. Once a study assistant has more to do, each job has its own procedure: how many review cards to make and in what format, which sections to split an error message into when turning it into a request for help, which kinds of input to cover when listing test cases for a function. The most direct approach is to write all of these procedures into the system prompt. This lesson calls that full injection.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: This lesson prepares four skills: review-cards, error-question, unit-test-checklist, and three-sentence-summary. With full injection, the system prompt is about 6,000 characters, and even if the user only says "Hi!", the request still carries all of them. Four skills isn't many. A made-up example: an assistant with 20 skills, each body 2000 characters, has a system prompt of 40,000 characters, while one request usually needs only one of them, or none at all.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: This costs you three ways. {{lesson:context-budget}} explained that the context window is limited and every request's tokens are billed, so resident bodies take up both space and money. {{lesson:prompt-caching}} explained that an unchanged start can hit the cache, which is cheaper and faster, but the cache doesn't take this text out of the context window. The third cost is the hardest to measure: procedures unrelated to the current task sit in front of the model all the time, and it may apply the review-card format to an ordinary question. This lesson compares another approach: give only a catalog first, and load a skill's body when that skill is needed.

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: A skill is a written procedure for the model, in two parts: a header and a body. Open locales/skills/review-cards/en.md: the header is between the two --- lines at the top and has only two fields. name is the skill's name and also the parameter load_skill takes; description says in one sentence when to use it, what the input is, and what the output is, and also when not to use it.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: After the second --- comes the body: when to use it, a four-step procedure, the output format (each card is a "Q:" line and an "A:" line), and a self-check before delivery. It is like a one-page instruction sheet handed to a new colleague: follow it and you produce review cards in a consistent format. The body is useful only when making review cards; replying to a greeting uses none of it. You can see the full file in the Code scene.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: A skill is not the same thing as a tool. A tool is a piece of code that the program executes and that returns a result. A skill is only text: the model reads it and follows it itself, and no code runs because of it. This lesson's load_skill is a tool, but what it does is simple: it reads a skill's body and hands it to the model. The review cards in the end are written by the model, not by load_skill.

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: Progressive disclosure splits a skill into two layers: only the catalog stays resident, and the body is supplied when needed. In the system prompt each skill takes just one line of name and description. The catalog for this lesson's four skills, together with the introductory text, is about 1,400 characters; the bodies stay in files. The model is also given a load_skill tool with a single parameter, name.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: It works like using a reference book: look at the table of contents first, find the entry, and turn to that page. Nobody reads from the first page to the last. After reading the user's task, if the model thinks it matches some skill's description, it proposes a call to load_skill. The runner reads the matching SKILL.md and puts the body back into the message history as a tool result, and the model completes the task by that body in the next request. If it thinks none match, it answers directly and loads no skill at all.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: When a skill is needed, request 2 of on-demand loading carries four messages: system is the catalog, user is the task, assistant is the proposed load_skill call, and tool is the body that came back. After reading these four, the model writes the review cards. The body is appended at the end, and not one character of the system prompt before it changes; we will use this when we discuss caching later. After each request, the runner emits a lesson.skill_request that records which skill bodies are in the messages just sent, so you can check one by one which request a body came in on.

deep-dive-layers.title.text: How real products layer and trigger skills

deep-dive-layers.summary.text: Beyond the catalog and the body there is often a third layer; products differ in what role the body takes when it enters the context.

deep-dive-layers.paragraphs.0.text: The skills in this lesson have only two layers. Real products often have three: the name and description in the catalog; the body of SKILL.md; and the sub-documents, templates, and scripts the body refers to, which are read further only when needed. Anthropic's Agent Skills are organized this way: SKILL.md starts with YAML metadata holding name and description, the body describes the procedure, complex details are split into other files in the same directory, and the body only says "read which file when needed".

deep-dive-layers.paragraphs.1.text: There is more than one way to trigger a skill, too. When the user types a slash command directly, the client can expand the body locally, with no need for the model to propose a call first. Only when the model decides on its own to use a skill is there an extra tool round trip, as in this lesson. Products also differ in what role the body takes when it enters the context. This lesson puts it in a tool result. Claude Code's documentation says it injects the body as a user message at the point of invocation. According to *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* (深入理解 AI Agent), OpenAI Codex regenerates the catalog every round.

deep-dive-layers.paragraphs.2.text: You can see both layers directly in Claude Code. A project's skills live in `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`. Normally only name and description enter the context, the body loads only when the skill is invoked, and reference files in the same directory come in only when the model goes to read them. The catalog itself has a character budget too: when there are too many skills, the least used ones lose their descriptions first. The user can type `/skill-name` to invoke a skill directly. With `disable-model-invocation: true` in the header, the description doesn't enter the catalog and the model never loads the skill on its own. The documentation also compares skills with `CLAUDE.md`: `CLAUDE.md` is loaded in full at the start of every session, which is like this lesson's full injection, while a skill's body comes in only when it is used.

deep-dive-layers.paragraphs.3.text: These implementations change fast; follow each product's own documentation. What doesn't change is the principle: a small catalog stays resident, the full body loads on demand, it is appended after what is already there when loaded, and the start that has already been sent is never edited afterward. The section on skill loading in Learn Claude Code demonstrates the same two layers with one tool and one catalog. It scans the whole skills directory and registers skills automatically; this lesson registers them explicitly instead, for the reason given in the next section.

deep-dive-tool-or-skill.title.text: Make it a tool, or write it as a skill

deep-dive-tool-or-skill.summary.text: The same capability can be written as a tool or as a skill; that is a separate decision from how many capabilities the model sees at once.

deep-dive-tool-or-skill.paragraphs.0.text: The same thing can be written two ways. Make "organize review cards" a tool and you write a function, constrain its parameters with JSON Schema, and the program returns the cards after executing. Write it as a skill and you have a procedure the model reads and follows. A tool's result is deterministic and testable, but every new capability means another piece of code and another tool definition. A skill is quick to write and people who don't program can edit it, but execution is left entirely to the model, and whether it came out right has to be checked separately.

deep-dive-tool-or-skill.paragraphs.1.text: This is a separate question from the one this lesson compares. The form a capability takes decides how much context each capability uses and who executes it; full injection versus on-demand loading decides how many capabilities the model sees at once. With many tools you can also give only a catalog and provide the definition when needed; with few skills, keeping them all resident is reasonable. The part of *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* that covers tools discusses these two decisions separately; this lesson looks only at the second one.

predict-load.prompt.text: After reading this far you can go to the lab bench for the first run. Before you run "Make review cards: both modes compared", guess how many tool_call events for load_skill this run will produce.

mq-catalog.what-model-sees.prompt.text: With on-demand loading, what can the model see of review-cards in request 1?

mq-catalog.what-model-sees.a.feedback.text: Correct. The body appears in the next request as a tool result only after the model calls load_skill.

mq-catalog.what-model-sees.b.text.text: The full body, just placed after the catalog

mq-catalog.what-model-sees.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The system prompt of request 1 has only the catalog. The report's check "On-demand loading: request 1 has no skill body" is run against the messages actually sent.

mq-catalog.what-model-sees.c.text.text: Nothing; it can only guess at the skill's name

mq-catalog.what-model-sees.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The catalog lists each skill's name and description, and the model decides which to load from those.

mq-catalog.what-model-sees.explanation.text: The catalog is resident and the body is on demand: each layer does one job.

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: load_skill's parameter is written by the model, and the runner uses it only to look up the allowlist, never as a path. The easiest way to write it is to splice the parameter straight into a path and read that file, but the model could write any string at all. For example, if it writes ../../../local_config.py and the read function uses the parameter directly as a file path, the resulting path escapes the skills directory and points to the local config file that holds keys, in the project root.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: So the runner first checks the allowlist SKILL_NAMES. Only if the name is in it does it read the matching skill file under locales/skills. If it isn't, an error is raised, and execute_tool turns it into a structured error with ok set to false and hands it back to the model. The tool result for the call above says "There is no skill named ../../../local_config.py" and then lists the four names in the catalog, so the model can correct itself.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: The allowlist also guards the other end: a file added to the skills directory does not appear in the catalog on its own; it counts only once it is registered in SKILL_NAMES. Scanning the directory automatically would be easier to write, but this lesson still registers explicitly, because a skill's body goes to the model as is and the model follows it. A skill file nobody has reviewed is like code nobody has reviewed: it shouldn't take effect quietly.

section-5.title.text: The description decides whether a skill gets picked

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: With on-demand loading, the model's only basis for deciding which skill to load is the name and description in the catalog. It can't see the body when it decides, so however good the body is, an inaccurate description means the skill isn't picked. This lesson's review-cards has two descriptions. The precise version states when to use it (the user supplies the original study notes and asks for review cards), what it outputs (3–5 "Q:/A:" cards), and when not to use it (when there are no original notes). The vague version is just "Helps with studying.". The experiment changes only that one line; the body and the other skills stay the same.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: An inaccurate description shows up in two ways. A missed trigger: the task should use the skill, but the model doesn't load it and answers directly from its own understanding. A false trigger: the task shouldn't use the skill, but the model loads it anyway. There is a third case, where the model should use a skill but loads a different one, which this lesson records as loading the wrong skill. This lesson's "Review question" task asks about a single concept and gives no notes. The lesson holds that it shouldn't load review-cards, and uses it specifically to test for false triggers.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: A good description reads like a decision condition, not a feature blurb: say when to use it, what the input is, what the output is, and add a sentence on when not to use it. "Helps with studying." states a feature, and organizing notes, asking a review question, and asking for study advice all seem to fit. Also, name itself carries information. The name review-cards already hints at review cards, so changing only the description does not necessarily change the result; what happens depends on the events of your run.

deep-dive-description.title.text: Condition by condition: how a description rules out similar tasks

deep-dive-description.summary.text: Check the three tasks against the precise description and the vague one, condition by condition, and see where false triggers come from.

deep-dive-description.paragraphs.0.text: The precise description breaks into four conditions: the user supplies the original notes; asks for review cards; the output is 3–5 question-and-answer cards; and don't use it when there are no original notes. Check this lesson's three tasks against them one by one. "Make review cards" pastes notes about lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets, and asks for review cards, so all conditions are met. "Review question" only asks how lists and tuples differ and has no original notes, so the last condition rules it out. "Small talk" has nothing to do with review and fails the first condition.

deep-dive-description.paragraphs.1.text: With "Helps with studying." there is only one condition left to check against, and it is too broad: organizing notes is studying, asking a review question is studying, and only saying hello on a Friday is clearly unrelated. The model can only separate them by name and its own guess. Which task is most likely to be loaded by mistake? The one most like making review cards but not needing them: the review question. The experiment includes the "Review question" task precisely to test this.

deep-dive-description.paragraphs.2.text: The sentence about when not to use it is the easiest to leave out, and it is exactly what blocks false triggers. The way to write it is to name the closest counterexamples: review-cards says "for example for study advice, answering questions or writing summaries", and three-sentence-summary says not to use it when the user wants review cards or a section-by-section explanation. When the descriptions of two skills draw a line against each other, the model is less likely to choose wrongly between them. Don't make descriptions longer and longer to be safe, either: the catalog goes with every request, and this lesson's English descriptions are about 40 to 50 words each. Write them at several hundred words and the catalog is no longer cheap.

mq-trigger.which-is-false-trigger.prompt.text: Which of these counts as a false trigger?

mq-trigger.which-is-false-trigger.a.text.text: The user only asks "what is the difference between a list and a tuple", and the model calls load_skill to load review-cards

mq-trigger.which-is-false-trigger.a.feed.text: Correct. The task shouldn't use the skill, but the model loaded it, spending one extra round trip and the tokens of a body.

mq-trigger.which-is-false-trigger.b.text.text: The user pastes notes and asks for review cards, and the model doesn't call load_skill and writes the cards directly

mq-trigger.which-is-false-trigger.b.feed.text: Not quite. That is a missed trigger: it should have loaded the skill but didn't, even if the cards' format looks fine.

mq-trigger.which-is-false-trigger.c.text.text: The user pastes notes and asks for review cards, and the model loads three-sentence-summary

mq-trigger.which-is-false-trigger.c.feed.text: Not quite. The task did call for a skill; the model just chose the wrong one, which this lesson records as "wrong skill loaded".

mq-trigger.which-is-false-trigger.explan.text: The judgment rests on whether the task should use a skill and on what was actually loaded in the events, not on how good the answer looks.

section-6.title.text: One more round trip, in exchange for a smaller resident context

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: What on-demand loading saves is the resident cost; the price is one more request when a skill is needed. When a skill is needed, request 1 only has the model propose a load. Request 2 carries the catalog, the load_skill call, and the body, and that is the one that actually completes the task, so request 2 has one body's worth more prompt tokens than request 1. Every on-demand request also carries the load_skill tool definition, which counts toward prompt tokens too.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: A made-up example, counted in tokens: catalog 150, the full-injection system prompt 750 (four descriptions plus four bodies), the body of review-cards 150, the tool definition 80, the user's task 100. Full injection sends once, about 750 + 100 = 850. On-demand request 1 is about 150 + 80 + 100 = 330. Request 2 adds the call message and the body, about 330 + 30 + 150 = 510. The total is 840, about the same as full injection, with one more response to wait for. Switch to small talk and full injection is still 850, while on-demand loading is just request 1's 330.

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: So which is cheaper depends on two separate costs. Request 1's prompt tokens are the resident cost, paid by every task. The body's tokens and the extra request are paid only when loading happens. When there are few skills and nearly every request needs one, on-demand loading may total more; when there are many skills and most requests don't need them, the gap flips. The lab report's "Prompt tokens per request" and "Total prompt tokens" columns are these two costs. The values come from prompt_tokens in each response's usage, and "not reported" is written when there is none. The report doesn't count the extra response you wait for.

section-7.title.text: The resident catalog is the stable prefix

section-7.paragraphs.0.text: The system prompt of on-demand loading holds only the catalog, so as long as you don't add or remove skills or change descriptions, every request starts exactly the same way. {{lesson:prompt-caching}} explained that the provider's cache works only on a request start that is exactly identical, so a catalog like this belongs at the very front of the request. The loaded body appears later, in a tool result, and doesn't change anything before it.

section-7.paragraphs.1.text: The system prompt of full injection can also stay unchanged, but it is much longer, and changing the body of any skill changes the whole start, so all earlier cache is useless. With on-demand loading, changing one skill's body affects only the second half of the request that loads it. Only changing a description or adding or removing a skill changes the catalog. This lesson's report doesn't count cache. To see whether usage has cache fields and what their values are, read the response events yourself, as taught in {{lesson:prompt-caching}}.

mq-cost.which-is-cheaper.prompt.text: For the task of making review cards, which uses fewer prompt tokens, full injection or on-demand loading?

mq-cost.which-is-cheaper.a.text.text: It depends on two costs: the resident part paid every time, and the extra round trip and body paid when loading

mq-cost.which-is-cheaper.a.feedback.text: Correct. The numbers are whatever the report's "Prompt tokens per request" and "Total prompt tokens" columns say.

mq-cost.which-is-cheaper.b.text.text: On-demand loading is always fewer, because the system prompt is shorter

mq-cost.which-is-cheaper.b.feedback.text: Not quite. When a skill is needed there is one more request, and request 2 also carries the body. With few skills the total can be higher.

mq-cost.which-is-cheaper.c.text.text: Full injection is always fewer, because it makes only one request

mq-cost.which-is-cheaper.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Each of its requests carries all the bodies, including requests that don't need a skill; the more skills, the larger the resident part.

mq-cost.which-is-cheaper.explanation.text: When comparing, keep resident cost and on-demand cost apart, and trust only the numbers in usage.

section-8.title.text: Limits: read the events, not the answer

section-8.paragraphs.0.text: On-demand loading leaves "whether to use a skill" to the model, so whether a skill was used can only be judged from events. The model may do the task without loading anything, or load the wrong skill. A correct-looking answer doesn't mean the skill was used: on a missed trigger, the model may write decent cards from its own understanding; on a false trigger, the model may read the body's "When to use" section and switch to answering directly.

section-8.paragraphs.1.text: There are three places in the events to look: whether the tool_call contains load_skill and which name its parameter holds; whether ok in the tool_result is true; and skills_in_context in lesson.skill_request, which records which skill bodies were in the context for each request. The format screening in the report looks only at whether the answer resembles review cards and does not judge whether the content is right; the load verdict looks only at events. The two columns are written separately, and they may disagree.

section-8.paragraphs.2.text: Loading in this lesson relies on the tool_calls field, which we have used since {{lesson:tool-selection}}: the model proposes a call, the runner executes it, and the result goes back as a tool message. The next lesson, {{lesson:text-actions}}, goes back to an earlier approach: without that field, the model writes the action in plain text, and the program has to make it stop in the right place and then parse the action out.

misconception-full.claim.text: Putting every skill body in the system prompt is the safest: the model can see everything, so it won't fail to use one.

misconception-full.correction.text: Being able to see something doesn't mean using it correctly. With full injection the model still has to decide for itself which procedure applies. It may fail to use one, or apply the review-card format to an ordinary question, and every request pays tokens for bodies it doesn't need. On-demand loading also has missed and false triggers. With either approach you have to go back to the events and the answer to check; "it was all written in" does not prove it will be used.

walkthrough.description.text: A step-by-step account of how on-demand loading goes; the code is a simplified illustration. The evidence for this run is in the events at the lab bench.

walkthrough.step-1.title.text: The system prompt holds only the catalog

walkthrough.step-1.body.text: One line of name and description per skill, and the request also carries the load_skill tool.

walkthrough.step-2.body.text: The model decides the task matches the description of review-cards and proposes load_skill in tool_calls.

walkthrough.step-3.title.text: Check the allowlist, then read the file

walkthrough.step-3.body.text: Only if the name is in SKILL_NAMES is the matching SKILL.md read; otherwise a structured error is returned.

walkthrough.step-4.title.text: The body goes back into the message history

walkthrough.step-4.body.text: The body is appended to the message history as a tool result, and the model sees it only in the next request.

walkthrough.step-5.title.text: Complete the task by the body

walkthrough.step-5.body.text: The model answers in the output format given by the body; the runner checks the events to produce the load verdict and the format screening.

code-decision.title.text: load_skill looks names up in a table, and the body comes back as a tool result

code-decision.chosen.text: Both the catalog and load_skill accept only names registered in SKILL_NAMES. A name written by the model is checked against the allowlist first, the matching SKILL.md is read only if it is found, and a structured error is returned if not. The body goes into the message history as a tool result, after the catalog.

code-decision.path-argument.title.text: Let the model pass a file path directly

code-decision.path-argument.why_not.text: A path the model writes can escape the skills directory and read files that shouldn't be read, such as local config; looking up a name in a table avoids this at the root.

code-decision.inject-all.title.text: Full injection, with caching to cut the cost

code-decision.inject-all.why_not.text: Caching can reduce the cost and latency of a repeated start, but the bodies still occupy the context window, and procedures unrelated to the task stay in front of the model; change one skill and the whole start changes.

code-decision.keyword-pick.title.text: Have the program pick skills by keyword first, then put the body in the system prompt

code-decision.keyword-pick.why_not.text: This is a workable approach, with clear rules and one less round trip. But the keyword table has to be maintained by hand, and a different wording slips past it. This lesson first looks at what happens when the model chooses by description.

full-vs-on-demand.hypothesis.text: For the same task, the system prompt of on-demand request 1 has only the catalog, so its prompt tokens are fewer than full injection's. When a skill is needed there is one more load_skill round trip, and the body appears in request 2. When no skill is needed, nothing is loaded and only one request is sent.

full-vs-on-demand.cards.label.text: Make review cards: both modes compared

full-vs-on-demand.full-system.text.text: The system prompt for full injection: the bodies of all four skills are in it.

full-vs-on-demand.full-record.text.text: The prompt tokens of this full-injection request; null if not reported, in which case the report says "not reported".

full-vs-on-demand.catalog-system.text.text: The system prompt of on-demand request 1: only the catalog.

full-vs-on-demand.catalog-record.text.text: The record of on-demand request 1: skills_in_context is empty, and prompt_tokens is lower than full injection's.

full-vs-on-demand.load-call.text.text: The load_skill call the model proposed, and the name it filled in.

full-vs-on-demand.load-result.text.text: The body the runner read, returned as a tool result.

full-vs-on-demand.second-record.text.text: The request after the body arrived: review-cards is now in skills_in_context, and the prompt tokens have grown by one body.

full-vs-on-demand.report-table.text.text: The two modes side by side: prompt tokens per request, total, load log, load verdict, and format screening.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.0.text.text: Each of the two arms runs both modes: request 1 is full injection, and on-demand loading starts from request 2. First look at what full injection sent.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.1.text.text: The bodies of all four skills are in the system prompt, whether the task needs them or not.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.2.text.text: These are the prompt tokens the provider reported; full injection pays this much on every request.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.3.text.text: The on-demand system prompt has only the catalog, one line per skill.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.4.text.text: No skill body is in this request's context. Compare with the prompt tokens of the previous record.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.5.text.text: When making review cards, the model should propose loading review-cards. In the small-talk arm, check whether this step happens.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.6.text.text: The runner checked the allowlist, read the body of SKILL.md, and returned it as a tool result.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.7.text.text: The next request carries the body, and prompt tokens grow with it. This is the extra cost of on-demand loading.

full-vs-on-demand.guide.8.text.text: The report puts the two modes side by side: compare the request 1 and total columns, then look at the load verdict.

full-vs-on-demand.conclusion.proves.0.text: In this run, how many requests each mode sent and how many prompt tokens each had (taken from usage; with no report, there is no number).

full-vs-on-demand.conclusion.proves.1.text: On-demand loading brings the body into the context only after the model proposes load_skill, and each request's skills_in_context can be checked one by one.

full-vs-on-demand.conclusion.does_not_pr.text: This lesson has only four short skills, so it can't represent the gap between the two modes when there are many skills with long bodies.
Prompt tokens show only the size of the request, not the quality of the answer.
Responses in offline test mode have no usage and don't represent the choices of any real model.

description-precision.hypothesis.text: Only the description of review-cards changes. With the precise description, the model loads it when organizing notes and doesn't load it for a review question; after switching to "Helps with studying.", the model may miss a load or load by mistake. Whether that happens shows in the tool_call of load_skill.

description-precision.catalog-line.text.text: The skill catalog in request 1: whether the review-cards line is the precise version or "Helps with studying.".

description-precision.first-decision.tex.text: The record after response 1: whether proposed_loads contains review-cards.

description-precision.load-call.text.text: The load_skill call: if it appears on the review question, it is a false trigger.

description-precision.verdict.text.text: The load verdict and format screening in the report: the two columns may disagree.

description-precision.final-answer.text.text: The final answer: from it alone you can't tell whether the skill was loaded.

description-precision.guide.0.text.text: The four arms differ in just two places: the task, and the description of review-cards. First look at that description line.

description-precision.guide.1.text.text: To decide which skill to load, the model can see only this catalog.

description-precision.guide.2.text.text: Whether the model proposed a load in response 1 is recorded in proposed_loads.

description-precision.guide.3.text.text: On making review cards, this being absent is a missed trigger; on the review question, this being present is a false trigger.

description-precision.guide.4.text.text: The load verdict looks only at events and the format screening looks only at the answer; the two columns are written separately.

description-precision.guide.5.text.text: The answer itself may be perfectly normal. To tell whether the skill was used, go back to the events above.

description-precision.conclusion.proves..text: In this run, whether the model loaded review-cards under the precise and the vague description, and in which request the loading happened.
The load verdict and the format screening can disagree: from the answer alone, you can't tell whether the skill was loaded.

description-precision.conclusion.does_no.text: Each arm runs once, so you can't see a trigger rate; running the same arm again may give a different result.
"Should it load or not" is this lesson's own judgment for these three tasks; with different tasks and skills, the standard has to be set again.
Missed and false triggers in offline test mode are scripted and don't represent any real model.

inputs.mode.options.both.label.text: Run both: full injection first, then on-demand loading

inputs.task.options.chat.label.text: Small talk (should not load a skill)

inputs.task.options.review_question.labe.text: Review question (should not load; easy to false-trigger)

inputs.description.help.text: Changes only the review-cards line in the catalog; the body and the other skills stay the same.

quiz.q-path.prompt.text: True or false: with on-demand loading, the runner splices load_skill's parameter into a file path and reads that file directly.

quiz.q-path.wrong.feedback.text: Correct, the statement is false. The runner first checks the allowlist SKILL_NAMES, and if the name isn't in it, returns a structured error and doesn't read any arbitrary path.

quiz.q-path.right.feedback.text: Not quite. If the parameter were spliced into a path directly, a name like ../../../local_config.py could read a file that shouldn't be read.

quiz.q-path.explanation.text: A string written by the model is used only to look up a table, and a registered file is read only if the lookup succeeds.

quiz.q-format.prompt.text: True or false: if the answer is written as 4 "Q:/A:" cards, the model must have loaded review-cards.

quiz.q-format.wrong.feedback.text: Correct, the statement is false. The model can write cards without loading anything, which is exactly why missed triggers are hard to spot.

quiz.q-format.right.feedback.text: Not quite. The format screening looks only at how the answer looks; only tool_call and tool_result can prove whether the skill was loaded.

quiz.q-format.explanation.text: The load verdict looks at events and the format screening looks at the answer; neither can stand in for the other.

quiz.q-resident.prompt.text: True or false: with full injection, even if the user only says "Hi!", the request still carries all the skill bodies.

quiz.q-resident.right.feedback.text: Correct. The bodies are in the system prompt and are sent with every request. The report's check "Full injection: the request carries every skill body" is run against the actual messages.

quiz.q-resident.wrong.feedback.text: Not quite. Full injection doesn't distinguish tasks, and the system prompt is just as long every time.

quiz.q-resident.explanation.text: The cost of full injection is resident, regardless of whether the task needs a skill.

quiz.q-total.prompt.text: True or false: when a skill is needed, on-demand loading's total prompt tokens are always lower than full injection's.

quiz.q-total.wrong.feedback.text: Correct, the statement is false. There is one more request, and request 2 also carries the body. With few skills the total can be higher; check the two columns in the report.

quiz.q-total.right.feedback.text: Not quite. On-demand loading saves the resident part paid every time, and when a skill is needed it pays for an extra round trip and a body.

quiz.q-total.explanation.text: Count resident cost and on-demand cost separately, and trust the numbers in usage.

quiz.q-when-not.prompt.text: The description of review-cards ends with "Do not use without original notes, for example for study advice, answering questions or writing summaries." What is this sentence mainly for?

quiz.q-when-not.a.text.text: To help the model rule out similar tasks that don't need this skill, reducing false triggers

quiz.q-when-not.a.feedback.text: Correct. When deciding whether to load, the model sees only the description, and naming the closest counterexamples keeps tasks like the review question out.

quiz.q-when-not.b.text.text: To tell load_skill to refuse to read the file for these tasks

quiz.q-when-not.b.feedback.text: Not quite. load_skill only checks the allowlist and doesn't read descriptions; the description is written for the model.

quiz.q-when-not.c.text.text: To make the body shorter and lower the prompt tokens of request 2

quiz.q-when-not.c.feedback.text: Not quite. This sentence is in the description, which stays resident in the catalog; it doesn't change the length of the body.

quiz.q-when-not.explanation.text: To pick a skill the model can see only the name and description in the catalog; a description that says clearly when to use it and when not to is what reduces both missed and false triggers.

quiz.q-vague.prompt.text: True or false: change the description of review-cards to "Helps with studying." and the model will definitely false-trigger.

quiz.q-vague.wrong.feedback.text: Correct, the statement is false. A vague description makes choosing harder, but name carries information too; whether a false trigger happened is seen in this run's tool_call.

quiz.q-vague.right.feedback.text: Not quite. Whether to load is the model's choice each time, and one run can't show "definitely".

quiz.q-vague.explanation.text: The description affects how likely a skill is to be picked; conclusions have to come from the events of many runs.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run "Review question: vague description" or "Make review cards: both modes compared" and find the step where the model proposes loading a skill.

check-hunt.explanation.text: The parameter of this tool_call names the skill the model wants to load, and the tool_result right after it is the body the runner read (or a structured error). The round it falls in is the request number given in the report's "Loading record" column. Finding it on the review question means a false trigger. If your run has no such event, the model loaded no skill at all this time; check the loading verdict in the report.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare your own run with this lesson's source code, and tick each item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: In the report of "Make review cards: both modes compared", I found the request-1 prompt tokens (or "not reported") and the total for both modes, and can say where they differ.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I can point out from which request the body of review-cards enters the context under on-demand loading, and which lesson.skill_request shows it.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I created a new skill in the skills directory (with name, description, and body), registered it in SKILL_NAMES, restarted the backend, ran "Small talk: both modes compared" again, and compared how much request 1's prompt tokens grew in each mode.

check-points.item-4.text.text: I set the lab bench task to "Small talk" and the description to "Vague", ran it again, and checked the load verdict for a false trigger.

code_notes.load_skill.note.text: The only tool in this lesson: looks up the allowlist by name and returns the body of SKILL.md; an unregistered name returns a structured error.

code_notes.SKILL_NAMES.note.text: The skill allowlist: only skills registered here enter the catalog and can be read by load_skill.

code_notes.description.note.text: The description field of SKILL.md. The catalog lists only it and name; the experiment changes only this one for review-cards.

code_notes.lesson.skill_request.note.text: The record after each request: prompt tokens, the skill bodies in the context, and the skills the response proposed loading.

code_notes.skills_in_context.note.text: The skill bodies found in the messages actually sent; for on-demand request 1 it should be empty.

code_notes.prompt_tokens.note.text: The prompt token count the provider reports in usage; null when not reported, and the report says "not reported".
